courses.title: Algebra & Number Sense
courses.summary: Linear relations and units, equations, inequalities, exponents, function notation, systems, and number sense — the highest-frequency ACT math skills.

skills.title: Linear Relations & Units
skills.key: Match every quantity to its unit rate. Convert mg to g before combining: $120\text{ mg}=0.12\text{ g}$. Days equal each total divided by its daily rate, then add.

skills.title: Number Properties & Divisibility
skills.key: A number is divisible by 3 exactly when its digit sum is. Bound digit puzzles first: if $A=(B+C)^2 \le 9$, then $B+C \le 3$.

skills.title: Custom Notation
skills.key: Treat a defined symbol as an equation. Unpack it, solve for the unknown, then evaluate what is asked — never the intermediate value.

skills.title: Solving Equations
skills.key: Undo operations in reverse order. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other until the variable stands alone.

skills.title: Solving Inequalities
skills.key: Solve like an equation — but flip the sign whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative.

skills.title: Exponents
skills.key: Same base multiply: add exponents. Coefficients multiply normally: $(2x^3)(3x^{-1})=6x^2$.

skills.title: Function Notation
skills.key: $f(4)$ means replace every $x$ with 4, then compute. Do not add the x's — evaluate the expression.

skills.title: Systems of Equations
skills.key: Add or subtract the equations to kill one variable. Adding $x+y=10$ and $x-y=4$ gives $2x=14$.

skills.title: Percentages
skills.key: Original = sale price $\div$ (1 $-$ discount rate). A 20% discount means you paid 80%: $\text{original}=48 \div 0.8$.

skills.title: Mean
skills.key: Total = average $\times$ count. Add the new score to the old total, then divide by the new count.

lesson.p: Every quantity has a unit. The number-one algebra trap is mixing them — milligrams with grams, minutes with hours, percent with decimals. Convert first, combine second.

list: Convert first: $120\text{ mg} = 0.12\text{ g}$. Never add grams to milligrams.
Days (or trips, or batches) equal each total divided by its rate, then add.
Read what each letter stands for before touching the options.

lesson.p: Divisibility by 3 looks only at the digit sum — never do the division. For digit puzzles, bound the possibilities first: a squared digit sum above 9 is impossible, so only a few cases survive.

list: Divisible by 3 if and only if the digit sum is divisible by 3.
If $A=(B+C)^2\le 9$, then $B+C$ is 2 or 3 — at most three cases to check.
List every surviving case ($411$, $912$, $921$) and test each one.

lesson.p: A defined symbol is an equation in costume. Unpack it, solve for the unknown, then answer exactly what is asked — often not the unknown itself. Function notation works the same way: substitute, then compute.

list: $f(4)$ means replace every $x$ with 4: $16-12+2=6$.
Never compute the intermediate value and stop — re-read the final ask.

lesson.p: Isolate the variable by undoing operations in reverse order. Inequalities behave identically — with one exception that the test loves.

list: $3x-1=2x+1$ gives $x=2$: collect variables left, constants right.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips $<$ to $>$: $-2x<6$ means $x>-3$.
Adding or subtracting never flips the sign — only $\times$ and $\div$ by negatives.

lesson.p: Multiply coefficients normally; combine exponents by rule. Same base, multiplying: add. Power to a power: multiply. Negative exponent: flip.

list: Never add coefficients to exponents — $2x^3$ times $3x$ is not $5x^4$.

lesson.p: Add or subtract whole equations to assassinate one variable. If the question asks for $y$, eliminate $x$ and stop — do not solve the full system.

list: $(x+y)+(x-y)=10+4$ gives $2x=14$, while subtracting gives $2y=6$.
Pick the operation that kills the variable you don't need.
Always plug back into the simplest equation to check.

lesson.p: Percent problems run backward: a 20% discount means 80% was paid. Mean problems run through the total: average times count, adjust, divide again.

list: $\text{original}=48\div 0.8=60$: divide by what you actually paid.
$\text{total}=\text{average}\times\text{count}$: $5\cdot 84=420$, then $\frac{420+96}{6}=86$.
20% off then 10% off is not 30% off — apply changes one at a time.
Units: convert before combining; $N=\frac{P}{50}+\frac{100V}{12}$.
Divisibility by 3: digit sum divisible by 3.
Functions: $f(a)$ means substitute $a$ everywhere.
Linear solve: reverse-order undo; inequality flips only on $\times/\div$ by negatives.
Exponents: $x^m\cdot x^n=x^{m+n}$, $(x^m)^n=x^{mn}$, $x^{-n}=\frac{1}{x^n}$.
Systems: add/subtract equations to eliminate one variable.
Percent: $\text{original}=\text{sale}\div(1-\text{rate})$.
Mean: $\text{total}=\text{avg}\times n$; new $\text{avg}=\frac{\text{old total}+\text{new}}{n+1}$.

problems.statement: Abe takes a daily supplement of either only protein or only vitamins. His daily intake is $50\text{ g}$ of protein and $120\text{ mg}$ of vitamins. After $N$ days, his total protein intake is $P$ grams and his total vitamin intake is $V$ grams. Which equation relates $N$, $P$, and $V$?
problems.explain: Convert first: $120\text{ mg}=0.12\text{ g}$. Protein days equal $P/50$ and vitamin days equal $V/0.12=V\div\frac{12}{100}=\frac{100V}{12}$. Add them: $N=\frac{P}{50}+\frac{100V}{12}$. B forgets the mg-to-g conversion.

problems.statement: In the three-digit number $ABC$, where $A$, $B$, and $C$ are digits from 1 to 9, $A$ equals the square of the sum of $B$ and $C$. How many such three-digit numbers are divisible by 3?
problems.explain: $A=(B+C)^2\le 9$ forces $B+C=2$ or $3$. That gives $411$ (digit sum 6), $912$ (sum 12), and $921$ (sum 12) — all divisible by 3. Three numbers.

problems.statement: If the mixed number $Z\frac{2}{3}$ equals $\frac{8}{3}$, what is the value of $Z^2-3$?
A jacket costs $48$ dollars after a 20% discount. What was the original price in dollars?
If $3(x-2)+5=2x+1$, what is the value of $x$?
Which of the following is the solution set of $-2x+7<13$?
For all $x\neq 0$, $(2x^3)(3x^{-1})$ equals:
If $f(x)=x^2-3x+2$, what is $f(4)$?
If $x+y=10$ and $x-y=4$, what is the value of $y$?
The average of five test scores is $84$. If a sixth score of $96$ is added, what is the new average?
problems.explain: Old total is $5\cdot 84=420$. New total $420+96=516$ over 6 tests: $516\div 6=86$.

courses.title: Geometry & Trigonometry
courses.summary: Right triangles, SOHCAHTOA, radian measure, circles, slope, area, and similarity — diagram questions reward labeling before computing.

skills.title: Special Right Triangles
skills.key: 30-60-90 sides are $x$, $x\sqrt{3}$, $2x$ with the hypotenuse opposite 90°. Read which side is longest first.

skills.title: SOHCAHTOA
skills.key: $\sin=\frac{opp}{hyp}$, $\cos=\frac{adj}{hyp}$, $\tan=\frac{opp}{adj}$ — right triangles only.

skills.title: Radians & Degrees
skills.key: $180^\circ=\pi$ radians. Convert degrees before combining with radian terms.

skills.title: Circles
skills.key: $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ has center $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ — watch the signs.

skills.title: Slope & Perpendiculars
skills.key: Perpendicular slopes are opposite reciprocals: $\frac{3}{4}$ becomes $-\frac{4}{3}$.

skills.title: Area
skills.key: Trapezoid: $\frac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2)h$. Arc length: $\frac{\theta}{360^\circ}\cdot 2\pi r$.

skills.title: Pythagorean Theorem
skills.key: $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Memorize 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and their multiples.

skills.title: Midpoint
skills.key: Average the x-values and average the y-values: $\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$.

skills.title: Similar Triangles
skills.key: Same shape, scaled sides. Set a proportion: person over shadow equals tree over shadow.

lesson.p: On every diagram question, write the known sides, angles, and what is asked directly on the figure. Half of geometry errors are bookkeeping errors.

list: 30-60-90: short leg $x$, long leg $x\sqrt{3}$, hypotenuse $2x$.
SOHCAHTOA: $\tan(\theta)=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
Convert first: $180^\circ=\pi$, so $\frac{8\pi}{3}-\pi=\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
Circle $(x+2)^2+(y-5)^2=36$ has center $(-2,5)$ and radius $6$.

problems.statement: Which of the following equals $\frac{7\pi}{4}+\frac{4\pi}{3}-\frac{5\pi}{12}-180^\circ$?
Matt has a garden in the shape of a right triangle with one acute angle $30^\circ$. The longest side is $8\text{ m}$. What is the perimeter of the garden?
problems.explain: The hypotenuse is $8$, so the short leg is $4$ and the long leg is $4\sqrt{3}$. Perimeter: $8+4+4\sqrt{3}=12+4\sqrt{3}$ m.

problems.statement: In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $35^\circ$ and the side adjacent to it is $10$. Which is closest to the opposite side?
problems.explain: $\tan(35^\circ)=\frac{\text{opp}}{10}$, and $\tan(35^\circ)\approx 0.700$, so the opposite side is about $7.0$.

problems.statement: A line has slope $\frac{3}{4}$. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
problems.explain: Perpendicular slopes are opposite reciprocals: flip $\frac{3}{4}$ and negate to get $-\frac{4}{3}$.

problems.statement: What is the center of the circle $(x+2)^2+(y-5)^2=36$?
problems.explain: Standard form $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ has center $(h,k)$. Here $h=-2$ and $k=5$, with radius $6$.

problems.statement: A trapezoid has bases $6$ and $10$ and height $4$. What is its area?
In a circle of radius $9$, what is the length of the arc cut off by an $80^\circ$ central angle?
A right triangle has one leg $6$ and hypotenuse $10$. What is the other leg?
What is the midpoint of the segment joining $(2,8)$ and $(6,2)$?
A $6$-foot person casts a $9$-foot shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a $27$-foot shadow. How tall is the tree, in feet?

courses.title: Probability
courses.summary: Every probability theory the ACT tests — basic chance, complements, AND/OR rules, expected value, Venn diagrams, counting, permutations, and combinations — taught through 27 worked examples that grow harder as you go, plus a distinct 10-question practice set.

skills.title: Basic Probability
skills.key: $P=\frac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}$. Count what you want, count everything, divide.

skills.title: Complements
skills.key: $P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$. When a question says “at least one,” compute one minus the opposite.

skills.title: AND Rule
skills.key: Independent events multiply: $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$. Without replacement, update the fractions as you go.

skills.title: OR Rule
skills.key: Mutually exclusive: add. General case: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ — subtract the overlap once.

skills.title: Expected Value
skills.key: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add: $E=x_1P_1+x_2P_2+\cdots$.

skills.title: Venn Diagrams
skills.key: Overlap means BOTH. Only-A equals A minus the overlap. Neither equals the total minus everybody counted.

skills.title: Counting Principle
skills.key: Choices multiply: $m\times n\times\cdots$. Digits, outfits, codes — same idea.

skills.title: Permutations & Combinations
skills.key: Order matters: permute ($n\cdot(n-1)\cdots$). Order irrelevant: combine (divide by the arrangements, $r!$).

lesson.p: Probability is a fraction: what you want over everything possible. Every harder rule below is just this fraction applied cleverly.

list: $P(\text{event})=\frac{\text{favorable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}$.
Simplify at the end, not the start — $\frac{4}{10}$ is easier to spot as $\frac{2}{5}$ after computing.
Probabilities always sit between 0 and 1; use that to kill absurd options.

lesson.p: “At least one” is a signal flare: do not enumerate the good cases. Compute one minus the single bad case.

list: $P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$.
“At least one head” in 2 flips: $1-P(TT)=1-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}$.
“Wrong answer” on a 5-option guess: $\frac{4}{5}$ — the complement of $\frac{1}{5}$.

lesson.p: AND narrows (multiply, number shrinks). OR widens (add, number grows) — but never count the overlap twice.

list: Independent AND: $P(A)\cdot P(B)$. No replacement across draws: update each fraction.
Mutually exclusive OR: just add, e.g. $0.4+0.25=0.65$.
General OR: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.

lesson.p: Expected value is a weighted average: each outcome times its probability, summed. Venn diagrams are the same OR rule drawn as circles.

list: $E=x_1P_1+x_2P_2+\cdots$. Losses enter with a minus sign.
Only-A = A − overlap. Neither = total − everybody counted.
Read the diagram before computing: shade what is asked.

lesson.caption: Two-set Venn: the overlap counts for both.

lesson.p: When stages are independent, multiply the number of choices at each stage. Repetition allowed means the same count repeats.

list: Outfits: $4\text{ shirts}\times 3\text{ pants}=12$.
Codes with repetition: $10^4=10{,}000$ for a 4-digit PIN.
Mixed alphabets multiply: $26^2\cdot 10^3=676{,}000$ plates.

lesson.p: Ask one question first: does order matter? Medals and passwords — yes, permute. Committees and hands — no, combine by dividing out the $r!$ arrangements.

list: Permutation: $5\cdot 4\cdot 3=60$ ways to award gold, silver, bronze to 5 runners.
Combination: $C(8,3)=\frac{8\cdot 7\cdot 6}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1}=56$ committees.
No-replacement draws chain fractions: $\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}=\frac{1}{221}$.

lesson.p: Hard ACT probability stacks two rules: a complement around an AND, an expectation with a twist, or a Venn with three numbers to untangle. Solve inside-out.

list: Basic: $P=\frac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}$, always between 0 and 1.
Complement: $P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$; “at least one” $=1-P(\text{none})$.
AND (independent): multiply. Without replacement: update fractions each draw.
OR (exclusive): add. OR (general): $P(A)+P(B)-P(\text{both})$.
Expected value: $\sum x_iP_i$; losses are negative.
Venn: overlap = both; only-A = A − overlap; neither = total − union.
Counting: multiply choices stage by stage; repetition repeats the count.
Permutations (order matters): $n(n-1)\cdots$. Combinations: divide by $r!$.
Dice/coins: list the sample space when small ($2^3=8$ for 3 flips).
Sanity: probabilities $>1$ or $<0$ mean a setup error — recheck.

examples.statement: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is $P(\text{red})$?
examples.discuss: Favorable is 5 red; total is $5+3=8$. So $P=\frac{5}{8}$. Always count the total first.

examples.statement: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
examples.discuss: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6 — 2 favorable out of 6 faces: $\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$. Simplify only at the end.

examples.statement: A spinner has 8 equal sectors, 3 shaded. What is $P(\text{shaded})$?
examples.discuss: $\frac{3}{8}$. “Equal sectors” is the license to use favorable-over-total — without it, you cannot.

examples.statement: From the letters of MATH, one is picked at random. What is the probability it is a vowel?
examples.discuss: Letters are M, A, T, H — one vowel out of four: $\frac{1}{4}$. Small sample spaces can be listed by hand.

examples.statement: If $P(\text{rain})=0.3$, what is $P(\text{no rain})$?
examples.discuss: Either it rains or it does not, so $P(\text{no rain})=1-0.3=0.7$. Complements always sum to 1.

examples.statement: Guessing on a 5-option question, what is the probability of being wrong?
examples.discuss: $P(\text{right})=\frac{1}{5}$, so $P(\text{wrong})=1-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{4}{5}$. Wrong answers are just the complement.

examples.statement: A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. One draw: what is $P(\text{not green})$?
examples.discuss: Direct count gives $\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}$; complement agrees: $1-\frac{4}{10}=\frac{3}{5}$. Two roads, same answer — use either to check.

examples.statement: Events A and B are independent with $P(A)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $P(B)=\frac{1}{3}$. What is $P(A\text{ and }B)$?
examples.discuss: Independent AND means multiply: $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{6}$. “Independent” is doing real work — without it, do not multiply blindly.

examples.statement: A and B cannot both happen, with $P(A)=0.4$ and $P(B)=0.25$. What is $P(A\text{ or }B)$?
examples.discuss: “Cannot both happen” means mutually exclusive, so just add: $0.4+0.25=0.65$. Nothing to subtract.

examples.statement: In a class of 30, 18 take math, 15 take science, and 8 take both. If one student is picked, what is $P(\text{math or science})$?
examples.discuss: General OR subtracts the double-counted overlap: $\frac{18+15-8}{30}=\frac{25}{30}=\frac{5}{6}$. Forgetting the 8 is the classic trap.

examples.statement: A die roll: what is $P(\text{even or greater than 4})$?
examples.discuss: Evens are 2, 4, 6; greater than 4 are 5, 6. Union is 2, 4, 5, 6 — four faces: $\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}$. The 6 sits in both sets, counted once.

examples.statement: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two draws with replacement: what is $P(\text{red then blue})$?
examples.discuss: “With replacement” resets the bag, so multiply unchanged fractions: $\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{6}{25}$. Order matters here — red-then-blue is one specific sequence.

examples.statement: A game pays $10$ with probability $\frac{1}{6}$ and $0$ otherwise. What is the expected payout?
examples.discuss: Weight each outcome: $10\cdot\frac{1}{6}+0\cdot\frac{5}{6}=\frac{10}{6}\approx\$1.67$. Expected value is a long-run average, not a possible single payout.

examples.statement: Of 100 people, 60 drink coffee, 50 drink tea, and 30 drink both. How many drink neither?
examples.discuss: Union is $60+50-30=80$; neither is $100-80=20$. (Only-coffee is 30, only-tea is 20 — handy checks.)

examples.statement: A quiz gives $+5$ per correct answer (probability $0.8$) and $-2$ per wrong answer. What is the expected score per question?
examples.discuss: Losses enter negative: $5(0.8)+(-2)(0.2)=4-0.4=3.6$. Dropping the minus sign is the standard miss.

examples.statement: A raffle sells 200 tickets for a $100$ prize; you hold 5. What is the expected value of your tickets?
examples.discuss: Win probability is $\frac{5}{200}$; $\frac{5}{200}\cdot 100=\$2.50$. Compare against the ticket price to judge the deal.

examples.statement: A closet has 4 shirts and 3 pants. How many shirt-pants outfits are possible?
examples.discuss: Independent stages multiply: $4\times 3=12$. Each shirt pairs with every pant.

examples.statement: A plate has 2 letters (26 each) followed by 3 digits (10 each). How many plates are possible?
examples.discuss: $26\cdot 26\cdot 10\cdot 10\cdot 10=26^2\cdot 10^3=676{,}000$. Same digit or letter may repeat unless told otherwise.

examples.statement: How many 4-digit PINs are possible if digits may repeat?
examples.discuss: $10\cdot 10\cdot 10\cdot 10=10^4=10{,}000$. “May repeat” keeps every stage at 10.

examples.statement: Five runners compete for gold, silver, and bronze (no ties). How many outcomes?
examples.discuss: Medals make order matter: $5\cdot 4\cdot 3=60$. Filling positions one by one is the permutation move.

examples.statement: How many 3-person committees can be chosen from 8 people?
examples.discuss: Order is irrelevant, so divide out the $3!=6$ arrangements: $\frac{8\cdot 7\cdot 6}{6}=56$. Committee = combination.

examples.statement: How many 4-digit PINs use distinct digits chosen from 6 available digits?
examples.discuss: Positions matter and digits cannot repeat: $6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3=360$. Contrast with Example 19, where repetition was allowed.

examples.statement: Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is $P(\text{both aces})$?
examples.discuss: Update the fractions after the first draw: $\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}=\frac{12}{2652}=\frac{1}{221}$. Forgetting to shrink 52 to 51 is the trap.

examples.statement: Three fair coins are flipped. What is $P(\text{at least one head})$?
examples.discuss: Eight equally likely outcomes, only TTT fails: $1-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{7}{8}$. Listing HHH, HHT, … confirms the single bad case.

examples.statement: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two draws without replacement: what is $P(\text{both red})$?
examples.discuss: Chain with shrinking totals: $\frac{5}{8}\cdot\frac{4}{7}=\frac{20}{56}=\frac{5}{14}$. Both the numerator and denominator move.

examples.statement: A 10-question quiz is guessed blindly (5 options each, $+1$ per correct, $0$ otherwise). What is the expected total, and what is $P(\text{all wrong})$?
examples.discuss: Per question $E=\frac{1}{5}$, so ten give $10\cdot\frac{1}{5}=2$ points. All wrong needs ten straight misses: $\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{10}\approx 0.107$.

examples.statement: Of 50 students, 30 are in band, 25 in choir, and 12 in both. How many are in band only, choir only, and neither?
examples.discuss: Band only: $30-12=18$. Choir only: $25-12=13$. Union: $18+13+12=43$, so neither is $50-43=7$. Three numbers, one subtraction each.

problems.statement: A jar holds 6 black and 4 white marbles. One is drawn at random. What is $P(\text{white})$?
A factory finds $4\%$ of parts defective. If one part is picked, what is the probability it works?
problems.explain: Working is the complement of defective: $1-0.04=0.96$.

problems.statement: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. What is $P(\text{heads and a 6})$?
A spinner has 10 equal sectors: 3 red, 2 blue, 5 green. What is $P(\text{red or blue})$?
problems.explain: Colors are mutually exclusive, so add: $\frac{3}{10}+\frac{2}{10}=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}$.

problems.statement: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is $P(\text{heart or king})$?
problems.explain: 13 hearts plus 4 kings, minus the king of hearts counted twice: $\frac{13+4-1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}$.

problems.statement: A game pays $\$5$ with probability $0.2$ and loses $\$1$ otherwise. What is the expected net gain per play?
A restaurant offers 2 soups, 5 mains, and 3 desserts. How many different three-course meals are possible?
In how many orders can 4 different books be arranged on a shelf?
In how many ways can 2 students be chosen from 6 for a project?
A club has 7 men and 5 women. Two different officers are chosen at random. What is the probability both are women?
